html:
The map's label for the peoples of the Pacific coast of North America, from southern Alaska to California, shown from 1500 BCE to 1500. They show that farming is not needed for dense, settled and ranked societies.

On the Northwest Coast, life rested on salmon. Huge runs came up the rivers each year, and people dried and smoked the fish to last the winter, adding fish oil, shellfish and sea mammals. Western red cedar gave them big plank houses, ocean-going dugout canoes and carved totem poles. Societies had nobles, commoners and slaves, and families showed their rank by giving away goods at the potlatch.

Peoples of this coast include:

  • the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian in the north;
  • the Kwakwaka'wakw and the Nuu-chah-nulth, who hunted whales;
  • the Coast Salish and the Chinook further south.

In California, acorns were the staple, ground and soaked to remove their bitterness. Without farming, California held one of the densest populations in North America and dozens of languages. The Chumash built plank canoes and used shell beads as money.

After the period on the map, Russian, Spanish and British ships arrived in the late 1700s to trade for sea otter furs, bringing smallpox with them.
